claim: In October 2017, only 1,393 Patreon creators — about 2% — earned the US federal monthly minimum wage equivalent of $1,160 (based on $7.25/hour), and only 0.8% earned a $15/hour equivalent, out of a platform total of 79,420 creators.
stance_target: The claim that the share of creators earning a living wage on direct-monetization platforms is on the order of 1-2%, not double digits
scope_conditions: Patreon platform only; earnings month October 2017; United States federal minimum wage benchmark; measured from Graphtreon's scrape of public Patreon earnings data, not a survey
quoted_support: Of those creators, only 1,393 — 2 percent — make the equivalent of federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour, or $1,160 a month, in October 2017. Worse, if we change it to $15 per hour, a minimum wage slowly being adopted by states, that's only .8 percent of all creators.
region: United States benchmark applied to a global platform — US/Western-only wage threshold

claim: The Patreon minimum-wage statistic rests on an ambiguous denominator: Graphtreon could only observe the roughly 80% of creators who publicly disclose earnings, yet the same sentence expresses 2% against disclosers and 0.8% against 'all creators'.
stance_target: The precision of the widely-cited 'under 2% of Patreon creators earn minimum wage' figure
scope_conditions: Patreon, October 2017; 79,420 total creators of whom ~80% (~63,500) disclosed earnings; 1,393/79,420 = 1.75% while 1,393/63,500 = 2.19%
quoted_support: Boruta's numbers are based on the roughly 80 percent of creators who publicly share what they earn. Of those creators, only 1,393 — 2 percent — make the equivalent of federal minimum wage

claim: Because Patreon permits creators to hide their earnings and high-profile top earners commonly do so, the Graphtreon-based estimate is drawn from a non-random subset that systematically excludes some of the highest earners.
stance_target: The representativeness of public-disclosure-based creator earnings estimates
scope_conditions: Patreon, 2017; illustrated by Philip DeFranco, whose patron count was public but whose earnings were hidden despite ranking in the platform's top 20
quoted_support: Patreon lets creators hide the amount of money they are actually making, although the number of patrons is still public.
numbers: 13,823 patrons for Philip DeFranco with undisclosed earnings

claim: Patreon's share of creators earning over $100 a month collapsed as the platform grew: in 2016 roughly 31% of about 25,000 creators cleared $100/month, but by October 2017 the platform had 79,420 creators and under 2% cleared $1,160/month.
stance_target: The claim that creator entry dilutes per-creator earnings on fixed-demand platforms
scope_conditions: Patreon; 2016 figure from Patreon's own blog post cross-referenced with a Fast Company creator count; thresholds differ between the two years ($100/month vs $1,160/month) so the comparison is directional, not like-for-like
quoted_support: In 2016, Patreon boasted that 7,960 users were now making over $100 a month ... Around the same time, the company reportedly had 25,000 creators, meaning only 31 percent of Patreon's users were making over a hundred bucks.

claim: Patreon's founder created the platform after a video costing $10,000 and three months of work drew nearly 2 million YouTube views but returned only $963 in ad revenue, an effective yield of roughly $0.48 per thousand views.
stance_target: The claim that platform advertising revenue share alone cannot fund content production at professional cost levels
scope_conditions: Single case; YouTube ad network circa 2013; reported by Jack Conte, who had a commercial interest in the comparison
quoted_support: the video cost him $10,000 and three months to make and got nearly 2 million views, he said, but he made just $963 through YouTube's ad network.

claim: Patreon creators received about 90% of monthly earnings before the December 2017 fee restructuring, with 5% retained by Patreon and roughly 5% consumed by payment fees and taxes.
stance_target: Gross-versus-net accounting in creator earnings comparisons
scope_conditions: Patreon; pre-December 2017 fee structure; the announced per-pledge fee change was subsequently withdrawn after creator backlash
quoted_support: For years, creators received 90 percent of their monthly earnings: 5 percent went back to Patreon, the middle man, and the remaining 5 percent went to fees and taxes.

claim: Patreon acknowledged in 2017 that most of its creators did not earn a full-time wage, while continuing to market the platform on the promise that starving and artist need no longer be joined at the hip.
stance_target: The claim that platform marketing systematically overstates typical creator earnings outcomes
scope_conditions: Patreon spokesperson statement to The Outline, December 2017
quoted_support: "We realize not all creators yet earn a full-time wage, but many of them do," a Patreon spokesperson told me in an email.

claim: Reported reasons for creator disillusionment on Patreon centre on unpaid promotional labour performed off-platform, tier-maintenance workload that scales with monetization complexity, and comparison-driven anxiety, rather than on content quality.
stance_target: The claim that documented quit and scale-back reasons are structural and workload-driven rather than talent-driven
scope_conditions: Qualitative interviews with a small number of named Patreon creators, December 2017; not a representative sample
quoted_support: One thing I've noticed is that most of the work is done outside Patreon. I promote my page on social media and deliver it to my supporters by text message.
